document.description: SWITCHYARD V9.17 — corrects a false claim rather than adding a feature: panel 1047 said this build emitted no per-model provider cost, which is wrong. The family exists and is event-driven, so it is absent between provider reconciliations — absence, not zero. Per-model reported cost is now read with an explicit last_over_time lookback and paired with a reconciliation-freshness stat; rolling gauges are never summed with cumulative counters, currencies and cost classes stay separated, and max_over_time is never shown as current cost. Adds the measured attempts-per-served-request figure with its scope stated, the reconciliation staleness check, and a panel naming what cannot be attributed at all (per-candidate skips, llm_calls model attribution, exported headroom). Unchanged: the dated, non-live Google quota and usage evidence, the Cloud-project-versus-Switchyard denominator separation, and every prior disclosure. P11 release 2026-11-28 (`20261128T020526Z-79286007`, label `p11-ultra-out`): Nemotron Ultra removed from `smart-route` automatic dispatch — desired and admitted topology are now both 5/3/1/2 = 11 and the direct alias `direct-openrouter-nemotron-3-ultra-free` is preserved. This corrects the "Ultra still desired but held" note in the PICTURE-3 record, which is historical as of 2026-11-25.

panels.description: What the global OpenRouter account has left to spend, in USD, as OpenRouter itself reports it. This is the account balance, not a key's share of it. Red below $1: at that point the next few requests decide whether the account runs dry, and free-tier slugs would keep working while paid ones start failing.
panels.title: OPENROUTER REMAINING (GLOBAL ACCOUNT)

panels.description: The second OpenRouter account, a separate billing identity with its own credit. Shown on its own because one account running dry does not stop the other from serving, and adding the two would hide which one is nearly empty.
panels.title: OPENROUTER REMAINING (STEPHEN ACCOUNT)

panels.description: DeepSeek's balance in CNY, the only currency it holds. DeepSeek also publishes a USD series that is structurally zero — it keeps no USD balance — so that series is deliberately not shown as though it were a measured dollar amount.
panels.title: DEEPSEEK BALANCE (CNY)

panels.description: Remaining percentage of the primary five-hour allowance. This is a rate window that refills on a clock, not money: running it low throttles throughput without costing anything, and waiting restores it.
panels.title: OPENAI 5-HR REMAINING

panels.description: One row per provider account. `deepseek` reports a structurally-zero USD series because its account is denominated in CNY; the CNY balance is the authoritative figure, so the USD placeholder row is suppressed here rather than shown as a real zero. Credited, consumed and remaining are three separate figures and are never summed into one number.
panels.title: EVERY PROVIDER ACCOUNT — BALANCE, CREDIT, USAGE, READ INTERVAL

panels.description: Whether the account figures are still being refreshed. This is the health signal the read interval cannot provide: a provider whose reads have stopped keeps publishing its last known balance, which looks current while being an old observation. Rising `failed` with a flat `ok` is that condition. Google owner-project quota and usage coverage is not an account-read series: it is the dated, non-live evidence row 2, and it is deliberately not counted in this health table.
panels.title: ACCOUNT READ HEALTH

panels.description: Percentage of the five-hour allowance still available.
panels.title: 5-HR REMAINING

panels.description: Countdown until the five-hour window refills, as the provider reports it. Rendered as a duration, so it reads in minutes when close and in hours when not. It falls toward zero and then jumps back up at the reset.
panels.title: TIME TO 5-HR RESET

panels.description: Percentage of the weekly allowance still available. This window refills on a different schedule from the five-hour one, which is why the two are never combined into a single figure.
panels.title: WEEKLY REMAINING

panels.description: Countdown until the weekly window refills. Rendered as a duration, so a figure near a week reads in days and hours rather than as a raw second count.
panels.title: TIME TO WEEKLY RESET

panels.description: The five-hour window over time. Used and remaining are complementary, so the two lines always total 100 and cross at the halfway point; a rise in one is a fall in the other, not an independent event. Each downward slope is consumption and each vertical recovery is the window refilling.
panels.title: 5-HR WINDOW — USED AND REMAINING

panels.description: The weekly window over time, on its own refill schedule. A slower, deeper slope here than in the five-hour window is the expected shape: the same traffic spread across a much larger budget.
panels.title: WEEKLY WINDOW — USED AND REMAINING

panels.description: Both countdowns on one axis, in seconds. Each is a sawtooth: a long fall as the window is consumed, then a jump back to the full period at the reset. The jump is when capacity returns.
panels.title: RESET COUNTDOWNS OVER TIME

panels.description: Seconds between successful DeepSeek account reads - the polling cadence, not a health status. It is recorded only when a read succeeds, so a stalled provider leaves the last value standing rather than growing. Read health lives in the ACCOUNT READ HEALTH table and in section 7.
panels.title: ACCOUNT READ INTERVAL

panels.description: DeepSeek's remaining balance in CNY - the only currency this account holds.
panels.title: BALANCE (CNY)

panels.description: Net movement of the balance over 24h, signed. POSITIVE means the balance rose, which is a top-up exceeding consumption - not spending. NEGATIVE means consumption exceeded any top-up, which is the reading that represents money actually used. Deliberately not clamped at zero: clamping would report a top-up as no change and erase the very event an operator needs to see.
panels.title: 24H NET BALANCE CHANGE (CNY)

panels.description: Highest minus lowest balance in the window - how far the balance travelled, regardless of direction. This is what a top-up followed by spending looks like: a large range with a small net change. Shown beside the net figure because the two answer different questions.
panels.title: 24H BALANCE RANGE (CNY)

panels.description: The portion of the balance that came from payments. DeepSeek splits its balance into purchased and granted credit, and the split matters because granted credit typically expires while purchased credit does not.
panels.title: REMAINING — TOPPED-UP (CNY)

panels.description: The portion of the balance granted rather than purchased. Usually expires, so it is worth less than the same amount of topped-up credit.
panels.title: REMAINING — GRANTED (CNY)

panels.description: Topped-up plus granted, computed here from the components rather than read from a second gauge. It must equal the balance panel; a divergence means the provider changed how it splits the balance and the components no longer account for it.
panels.title: REMAINING — TOTAL (CNY)

panels.description: The low-water mark of the balance over 24h. This is the figure that says how close the account came to empty, which the current reading can hide if a top-up arrived in the last few minutes.
panels.title: LOWEST BALANCE IN 24H (CNY)

panels.description: The balance as sampled at each account read. Gaps in this line are missing telemetry, not zero balances: the series simply has no sample there, and the line is drawn broken rather than interpolated across them. A vertical jump upward is a top-up; a steady decline is consumption.
panels.title: BALANCE TREND (CNY)

panels.description: How the balance splits between purchased and granted credit. Granted credit expiring shows as a step down in the granted line that the topped-up line does not share - which is why the total can fall without any request having been served.
panels.title: BALANCE COMPONENTS OVER TIME (CNY)

panels.description: Polling cadence for the global account. Recorded only on a successful read, so it does not grow when reads start failing.
panels.title: GLOBAL — READ INTERVAL

panels.description: Remaining account balance. Shown to four decimals because the number that matters here is often a few cents — rounding to two would render a nearly-empty account as indistinguishable from an empty one.
panels.title: GLOBAL — REMAINING (USD)

panels.description: Cumulative consumption on the account since it was created. This is a lifetime figure and never decreases; it is not this month's spend, which is the panel near the end of this section.
panels.title: GLOBAL — TOTAL USAGE (USD)

panels.description: Total credit ever purchased for the account. Together with remaining balance it closes the accounting: purchased minus remaining should be the total usage.
panels.title: GLOBAL — PURCHASED CREDITS (USD)

panels.description: Cumulative usage now minus cumulative usage 24h ago — what was actually consumed in the window. Signed on purpose: a provider correction or reset that lowers the cumulative figure produces a negative value, which is the truth about the series rather than a fault to clamp away.
panels.title: GLOBAL — 24H SPEND (USD)

panels.description: Usage attributed to this key rather than the whole account. Lower than account usage when other keys also draw on the same credit — which is the normal case and not a discrepancy.
panels.title: GLOBAL — KEY USAGE (USD, CUMULATIVE)

panels.description: Consumption in the current calendar month, as the provider resets it. Distinct from total usage: this is the figure that matters against a monthly budget.
panels.title: GLOBAL — THIS MONTH (USD)

panels.description: Consumption in the current week, as the provider resets it. Useful for spotting a pace change before it shows up in the monthly figure.
panels.title: GLOBAL — THIS WEEK (USD)

panels.description: Consumption so far today. Zero is a real and common reading: it means nothing has been spent through this key yet in the provider's current day.
panels.title: GLOBAL — TODAY (USD)

panels.description: Remaining balance on the second OpenRouter account. A separate billing identity, not a view of the first: its credit is bought separately and runs out separately.
panels.title: STEPHEN — REMAINING (USD)

panels.description: Credit purchased for the Stephen account.
panels.title: STEPHEN — PURCHASED CREDITS (USD)

panels.description: Cumulative consumption on the Stephen account.
panels.title: STEPHEN — TOTAL USAGE (USD)

panels.description: Three views of one account. Usage climbs, credit is a step function that rises on each purchase, and remaining is bought minus consumed. The vertical gap between the credit line and the usage line is the money still available — the same number as the remaining panel, read geometrically. A step up in credit is a top-up; the remaining line should jump with it.
panels.title: GLOBAL ACCOUNT — USAGE, CREDIT AND REMAINING

panels.description: The same three measurements for the Stephen account, kept on their own axis range because its figures are an order of magnitude smaller and would otherwise look flat beside the global account.
panels.title: STEPHEN ACCOUNT — USAGE, CREDIT AND REMAINING

panels.description: The previous revision filtered `provider=~"openrouter.*"`, but this build emits no `provider` label on the rolling family, so that filter could only ever return nothing. Grouped by model, which is present.
panels.title: REQUESTS, ROLLING 24H, BY MODEL (ALL PROVIDERS)

panels.description: Input tokens as provider-counted, since the deployment started. This total already contains the cached and cache-created tokens, so those are shown beside it and never added to it.
panels.title: PROMPT TOKENS

panels.description: Output tokens as provider-reported. Reasoning is published separately by the providers that report it and is not added here, so each provider's own figures are preserved exactly.
panels.title: COMPLETION TOKENS

panels.description: Reasoning tokens where reported. Its relationship to completion varies by model — measured across the routing log, some models report reasoning above completion — so no arithmetic relationship is asserted. Absent means unreported, not measured zero.
panels.title: REASONING TOKENS

panels.description: Prompt tokens served from the provider's cache. Compared with the prompt total, this is how much input was not re-sent at full price.
panels.title: CACHED PROMPT TOKENS

panels.description: Input volume per model — the cost driver that scales with conversation length and the one routing can most directly move.
panels.title: PROMPT TOKENS BY MODEL

panels.description: Output volume per model with reasoning alongside rather than inside completion. Where both bars exist, the split shows how much of the work was deliberation.
panels.title: OUTPUT TOKENS BY MODEL — COMPLETION AND REASONING

panels.description: Today's tokens split by component, from one series so the whole is the sum of its parts as the binary recorded them.
panels.title: TOKEN COMPONENT MIX TODAY

panels.description: Rolling 24h tokens by component. A cached share growing while prompt stays flat is the usual sign that prompt reuse is working.
panels.title: TOKENS, ROLLING 24H, BY COMPONENT

panels.description: `switchyard_economics_requests_total` carries `model`, `cost_class` and `component` only. The previous title said 'by provider' but the label does not exist, so the chart showed one unnamed series. Grouped by cost class, which is emitted.
panels.title: REQUESTS BY COST CLASS (NO PROVIDER LABEL IN THIS BUILD)

panels.description: Requests per model. Read with the error table in section 6: a model carrying a large share of traffic and a high error rate is an active problem. Counts here are cumulative for the running Switchyard process and reset when it restarts, not a rolling 24h window; the panels titled “rolling 24h” are the windowed comparison.
panels.title: REQUESTS BY MODEL

panels.description: Grouped only by labels that are actually emitted. `route` and `provider` are NOT labels on these families, so any column naming them renders empty — an empty column is the absence of a label, not evidence that routing is unattributed. Provider-reported money was moved off this panel to the dedicated cost table further down, because it is event-driven and an instant query on it returns nothing between reconciliations.
panels.title: MODEL × COST CLASS — VOLUME AND TOKENS (24H ROLLING)

panels.description: Requests by the kind of route addressed — direct, primitive, tier or composite. Separates deliberate direct calls from traffic that arrived through a routing layer.
panels.title: REQUESTS, ROLLING 24H, BY COST CLASS

panels.description: Upstream attempts that did not return 2xx. Attempts, not requests: a request that retried twice and then succeeded contributes two here and nothing to the panel beside it. Confusing the two makes a healthy deployment look broken.
panels.title: UPSTREAM ATTEMPTS FAILED

panels.description: Failed attempts that a later attempt served. Upstream errors that never became a caller-visible failure.
panels.title: ATTEMPTS RECOVERED BY RETRY

panels.description: Responses delivered to callers that ended in an error, after every recovery opportunity was used. The only error count here a user would recognise as their own failed request.
panels.title: REQUESTS THAT REACHED A CALLER AS ERRORS

panels.description: Times the router found an entire account's allowance exhausted. Decided from the provider's structured error, not from the status code — the semantic signal that stops a request being retried against a credential already known to be empty.
panels.title: ACCOUNT-WIDE QUOTA BLOCKS

panels.description: Attempts grouped by the status received and the outcome the binary derived from that code alone. HTTP evidence, not a diagnosis: `429 retryable_error` covers both a genuine rate limit and an exhausted balance, because the status cannot tell them apart. The composition panels carry that distinction.
panels.title: UPSTREAM ATTEMPTS BY STATUS AND HTTP-DERIVED OUTCOME

panels.description: Attempt rate per status. A steady 429 line is pacing pressure retries can absorb; a 401 or 403 line is a credential or policy problem that cannot be retried away.
panels.title: UPSTREAM ATTEMPTS BY STATUS OVER TIME

panels.description: What the composition layer decided, by the capability it handled. This is the binary's own semantic classification and the most trustworthy error breakdown available: `credential_quota` means an allowance was known exhausted before a call was spent; `account_quota` means an account-wide limit was hit.
panels.title: COMPOSITION OUTCOMES BY CAPABILITY

panels.description: Requests that left one child route for another, with the classified reason. A large `account_quota` count against one child means that child's credential is routinely exhausted and the route is paying for a crossing it could avoid by reordering candidates.
panels.title: ROUTE CROSSINGS BY REASON

panels.description: Per-model failure rate with its denominator shown, so a 100% rate on two calls is not mistaken for a broken model. `clamp_min` keeps the division defined when a model has no calls; it does not manufacture a zero for an unused model.
panels.title: ERROR RATE BY MODEL

panels.description: The same rate as a trend, which distinguishes a model that has always been unreliable from one that started failing an hour ago — a change a cumulative rate would hide.
panels.title: ERROR RATE BY MODEL OVER TIME

panels.description: What callers actually received. `ok` beside a smaller `retryable_error` is recovery working; `other_error` growing without a matching upstream explanation points at a local failure — a translation or configuration problem — rather than a provider.
panels.title: CLIENT-VISIBLE OUTCOMES

panels.description: Routing runs and how they ended, by the algorithm that selected. A run can end differently from its upstream attempts because the algorithm may fall back.
panels.title: RUN OUTCOMES BY ALGORITHM

panels.description: Every client response in the last 5m, split by outcome. `ok` served, `retryable_error` a 429/5xx-class answer, `other_error` a request-level refusal, `client_disconnected` the caller hung up. An absent series is absent, not zero: the panel does not fabricate a zero for an outcome nobody produced. Bars are a single neutral colour on purpose: a table-backed barchart in Grafana 13 colours by FIELD, not by row, so a per-outcome palette here would be the default cycle and could paint `client_disconnected` green. The outcome label carries the meaning; the per-outcome colour legend lives in CLIENT OUTCOMES (15m) where every outcome really is a field.
panels.title: CLIENT OUTCOMES (5m) — COUNTS BY OUTCOME

panels.description: Successful provider account reads since this process started.
panels.title: ACCOUNT READS OK

panels.description: Account reads that did not succeed, for any reason. Computed as total reads minus successful reads rather than by filtering to a failing outcome, so a healthy deployment reads a real 0 instead of No Data, while a vanished metric family still leaves the panel empty. A rising count here means the balance figures above are ageing.
panels.title: ACCOUNT READS FAILED

panels.description: Times a provider rejected our own credential while reading account state. Event driven: the family appears only after the first occurrence, so an absent panel means none has been recorded in this process, not that measurement is broken.
panels.title: ACCOUNT READ FAILURES (total)

panels.description: How many provider accounts are being read at all. A provider missing here has no native financial instrumentation, so its absence from the account sections is a coverage gap rather than a zero balance.
panels.title: PROVIDERS WITH ACCOUNT COVERAGE

panels.description: Seconds of real observation behind every rolling 24h figure on this dashboard. After a restart this is below 86400 until the process has been up a full day; while it is, the 24h numbers describe a partial window and should not be compared with a full one.
panels.title: ROLLING 24H COVERAGE

panels.description: Distinct providers that have completed at least one account read in this process. A provider absent from the account sections entirely is a coverage gap, not a zero balance: it has no native financial instrumentation, so nothing is known about its money rather than everything being zero.
panels.title: PROVIDERS CURRENTLY REPORTING

**OUTPUT TOKENS — latest PROVABLY COMPLETE hourly bucket per model (Cloud Monitoring).**

Source: `generate_content_usage_output_token_count`, `ALIGN_SUM` over `3600s`, grouped by `metric.label.model`; read 2026-11-22T20:30:00Z. `bucket end` is the provider's own UTC window end, **not** the exporter scrape time — the age column is that bucket's age at the read.

**Completeness rule:** a bucket is only counted once its end is at least 65 minutes behind the read, because the measured provider lag is about an hour. 1 bucket(s) in this response ended inside that window and were **discarded as still moving** rather than published as a finished hour. That is why the tokens here differ from a naive "newest point" read, and the difference is the point of the panel: at V9.7 this row published a bucket that had ended less than a minute before the read (542 tokens for `gemma-4-26b`) where the closed bucket holds 11,796.

| model | bucket end (UTC) | age at read | output tokens | coverage in window |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` | 2026-11-22T16:29:31Z | 240 min | 16,982 | 4 of `4` bucket(s) provably closed |
| `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` | 2026-11-22T16:29:31Z | 240 min | 12,974 | 4 of `4` bucket(s) provably closed |
| `gemma-4-26b` | 2026-11-22T18:29:31Z | 120 min | 11,796 | 1 of `2` bucket(s) provably closed |

panels.title: COLLECTOR STATUS — PHASE B CREDENTIAL GATE

panels.content:
The OpenAI figures on this dashboard are **rate windows**, not money. A five-hour window at 18% remaining does not mean 82% of a budget has been spent and lost — it means throughput is currently throttled, and waiting restores it at no cost. That is why they are not added to the dollar figures anywhere on this dashboard, and why a low reading is a routing consideration rather than a financial event.

The two windows refill independently. A request can be refused by a nearly empty five-hour window while the weekly window is barely touched, so they are shown separately and never averaged.

**What the counter does when a reading cannot explain a reservation (2026-11-28).** A reading records the gap against its own watermark as `pending` and reclaims nothing at that moment; a later reading, at least the settlement delay after the one that found the gap, may reclaim only what the provider has not since counted. An unwatermarked reading declares **no claim** — it neither creates one nor carries an older one forward — and a settled gap is **discharged**, so the same units cannot be reclaimed twice, with `release_uncharged_at` shrinking the pending amount by what it releases. `spent` stays monotonic throughout: reclaimed units move to `uncharged`, which is what admission and watermark comparisons subtract. None of this is a savings claim — it is a correction to how an unexplained reservation is carried, and the provider's own later figure is the only evidence that settles it.

panels.content:
**CNY only.** DeepSeek keeps no dollar balance. It publishes a USD series that is structurally zero, and a panel reading it would show a confident `$0.00` for an account holding real money. It said `switchyard_economics_rolling_provider_cost` was not emitted by this build, and that `count(...)` returned an empty vector. The stat beside the table is the live test: when it is 0, the table is last-known, not current. - `switchyard_economics_calendar_provider_cost{provider}` — calendar-scoped, same event-driven cadence.

- `max_over_time` is never presented as current cost — by definition it is a historical peak.

panels.content:
Both OpenRouter accounts are shown because **they are separate billing identities**. `openrouter` and `openrouter_stephen` hold separately purchased credit; one running out does not affect the other, so merging them would hide which one is close to empty and would misstate the exposure.

Within one account, four figures are easy to confuse and are deliberately kept apart: **remaining** (what is left), **purchased credit** (what was ever bought), **total usage** (lifetime consumption) and **this month** (consumption inside the provider's current month). Remaining is not the difference between the other two unless no top-up has ever been partial, and this month is not a fraction of total usage in any fixed way.

panels.content:
`switchyard.economics_account_freshness_seconds` is recorded **only when a read succeeds**, and its value is the elapsed time since the previous success. Two consequences follow, and both matter for reading this dashboard.

It reports the **polling cadence** — roughly five minutes for a healthy provider — not the age of the balance on screen. A panel labelled "Status" showing `5 mins` was reporting the cadence, not saying the account was healthy five minutes ago.

It **cannot reveal staleness**. When reads start failing, no new value is recorded, so the gauge keeps its last interval and the panel goes on showing a healthy-looking number while the balance it describes gets older. That is why read health is shown from `account_fetch_total` by outcome instead: a flat `ok` count beside a rising failure count is the actual signal, and it is what section 1's ACCOUNT READ HEALTH table displays.

panels.title: THE ACCOUNT READ INTERVAL IS NOT A HEALTH STATUS

panels.content:
`switchyard_upstream_attempts_total` records one increment per attempt, labelled with the HTTP status received. Its `outcome` label is a **function of that status alone** — 408, 429 and 5xx become `retryable_error`, everything else `other_error`. It is honest about what it saw and silent about why.

Two cases the providers document explicitly are invisible in that label. A `429` may be a rate limit that clears in seconds or an exhausted balance that no retry can fix. An OpenRouter `500 server_error` may be masked infrastructure trouble or a permanent authentication failure reported only in the top-level `error_type`. Neither is recoverable from the status code.

The semantic classification that does exist natively is the composition layer: its `capability` and `reason` labels are decided from the provider's structured error. Section 6 shows both facts side by side rather than presenting one as the other.

panels.title: WHY THE TWO ERROR RATES DIFFER, AND WHY NEITHER IS A DIAGNOSIS

panels.content:
**Zero.** A series that exists and reads zero. The traffic, spend or balance is genuinely zero — `GLOBAL — TODAY` showing 0.00 is a real reading.

**No event observed.** A family that only appears once its event happens. Account authentication failures are the example: an empty panel means the event has not occurred in this process, not that measurement is broken.

**Partial window.** Rolling windows are computed by the binary from events it observed. After a restart the coverage panel drops below 86400s and the 24h figures describe less than a day. **Measured at the V9.4 save:** the release restarted the process at 2026-11-22T15:37:16Z and `rolling_coverage_seconds{window="24h"}` read **480 s** at 15:45:50Z — about eight minutes of observation (109 requests), not a day. panels.content:
### WHAT THESE NUMBERS ARE, AND WHAT THEY ARE NOT

**Attempts per served request is not a refusal rate.** The denominator counts only requests that
were *served*; a failed request never enters it. The numerator counts actual HTTP sends to a
provider. A ratio near 1.0 therefore means "for the requests that were served, roughly one upstream
send each". It does not measure retries, local refusals, or candidate skips.

**No per-candidate skip or refusal counter exists in this build.** Candidate refusal, eligibility
skips and allowance-gated skips are counted nowhere. Nothing on this dashboard stands in for them.

**`llm_calls` cannot attribute a failure to a model.** `record_llm_call` labels `selected_model`
with `models.first()` — the head of the candidate list, not the model that served or failed. Three
distinct free models carry identical error counts, which is the signature of list-head labelling.
The ERROR RATE BY MODEL panel above inherits this caveat and is not a per-model failure ranking.

**Headroom is partly a series (corrected 2026-11-27).** Raw account balance, purchased credit, period-scoped usage, per-account freshness and the subscription allowance percent/reset ARE exported - panel 1047 carries the measured inventory and its authority table. What is not a series is **effective** headroom (balance minus spend since the reconciliation anchor): spend is exported only as period snapshots, with no monotonic currency counter and no exported anchor timestamp, so `balance − usage{period="daily"}` is neither a value nor a bound of known direction (the balance is already net of spend at reconciliation, so the subtraction can double-count or omit spend). Until that is instrumented, no panel may present a derived headroom figure as fact.

### CURRENT-SCOPE NOTE (2026-11-27)

The attribution limit above is unchanged in the deployed build. `selected_model` on `switchyard_llm_calls_total` is the **candidate list head**, so panels 1072/1073 attribute an error to the head model, not to the model that actually failed or served. Read them as list-head attribution only. Actual serving evidence is the `final_target` field in the routing log, not these series. Historical rolling-24h aggregates on this dashboard are **not** current activity; the current process interval is the only current measure.

**Source-level confirmation of the head-labelling (2026-11-27).** `libsy/src/core/algorithm.rs`, `CallModel::record()`, labels `switchyard.llm_calls` with `self.models.first()` — the candidate-list head. The doc comment on `CallModel` adds that a consumer falling through to a later candidate must re-stamp the *request*, which does not change the label. Consequence for the cost-containment read: the 24 h value reported on `deepseek-v4-pro` (1) is a list-head count, not a V4 Pro failure count. V4 Pro is the capable target — and therefore the model-list head — of the `[REMOVED P11: vc-paid-core]` auto route, and after the 06:33:10Z release it is otherwise reachable only through `direct-deepseek-deepseek-v4-pro`.

Historical rolling-24h aggregates on this dashboard are **not** current activity; the current process interval is the only current measure.

**Source-level confirmation of the head-labelling (2026-11-27).** `libsy/src/core/algorithm.rs`, `CallModel::record()`, labels `switchyard.llm_calls` with `self.models.first()` — the candidate-list head. The doc comment on `CallModel` adds that a consumer falling through to a later candidate must re-stamp the *request*, which does not change the label. Consequence for the cost-containment read: the 24 h value reported on `deepseek-v4-pro` (1) is a list-head count, not a V4 Pro failure count. V4 Pro is the capable target — and therefore the model-list head — of the `[REMOVED P11: vc-paid-core]` auto route, and after the 06:33:10Z release it is otherwise reachable only through `direct-deepseek-deepseek-v4-pro`.
